utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom, and also those assisting us in the interpreters' booth and the technical booth. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in respect of this witness, protective measures were ordered in another case, and they continue to exist. The protective measures are pseudonym and facial distortion, so for the entrance of the witness into the courtroom, we have to pull the curtains down.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's occurring, there's a number of matters I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I've raised with Ms. Karagiannakis an objection I have to an aspect of the summary, and Ms. Karagiannakis -- of course, the summary not being evidence -- that is agreed to excise that particular portion from the summary. The other aspect, Your Honour, is that my case manager has just been handed some documentation in relation to the -- the witness next Tuesday, and I would indicate that that's the first that the Defence knew that this particular witness would be called next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I've just had a discussion with Mr. Hannis in relation to this. I think it's unfortunate if the -- if we're given this sort of late notice. I understand that the circumstances are that this witness was taken off the 92 bis list, placed on the viva voce list, and what have you. But in any event, our first notification that this is the witness for next Tuesday is just now. And I'd just like to place that on the record, that this places the Defence under constant, enormous pressure in relation to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean that you would need more time to prepare for cross-examination or...?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't -- at this stage it has just been handed to us. I don't -- at this stage I don't even -- I haven't had a chance to have a look at the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a crime-based witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm assuming so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a crime-based witness. This is a witness from Kljuc Municipality which was one of the municipalities that we neared 90 per cent agreement on during the proposed agreed facts project. But we have no objection if after reviewing it and after the witness has testified the Defence requests some additional time to prepare for cross-examination, but we do think it's a relatively simple witness as witnesses in this case go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, I would then like to hear from you any further. The Chamber has discussed the schedule to come, and perhaps you would gain some extra time if we are dealing with quite a lot of, I would say, household matters, such as exhibits still to be discussed and to be admitted perhaps on Monday that might give you some extra time because I don't think that the whole of the Defence team would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Now, just in relation to the next witness, in addition, I would indicate that I would be -- as this is a witness under -- that is proposed to be dealt with under 89(F), and I would indicate that I would be proposing to object to the Bosnian statement. The -- I think there's two statements proposed to be tendered under the 89(F) procedure by the Prosecution. That's the statement under the auspices of the ICTY, and the second one being the Bosnian statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's first one of the 26th of August, and the 3rd of November. Although there seems to be some confusion as to the date in some respects.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The previous Bosnian statement under 1998. Of course, it's a discretionary matter for Your Honours, but taking into account the discussion of these matters in the Appeals Chamber decision from the Milosevic trial on the relationship between 89(F) and 92 bis, of course, Your Honour does have a discretion in relation to these matters. And, Your Honour, I would submit that the statement taken under the auspices of the ICTY as opposed to the statement taken in 1998 by the Bosnian authorities does, in fact, have all the hallmarks that are enumerated by 92 bis. And in those circumstances, and quite frankly, it doesn't add anything in my submission to the ICTY statement, that then I would be submitting areas in the realm of speculation, and in those circumstances I would be objecting to the Bosnian statement. And I also would note in this context that Your Honours already noted that the witness was subject to protective measures in the Brdjanin trial. In the Brdjanin trial, in the Brdjanin trail the approximate merely tendered the ICTY statement and not the Bosnian statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just to clarify what I'm going seek admission of in the first place. There are in fact two statements and one additional information provided by the witness. The first statement is the 31 March 1998 taken by AID. That's the first statement the witness ever gave about the events in the municipality. The second statement is -- was taken on the 26th of August and the 3rd of November 1999. So that's the ICTY statement. And then you have the additional memorandum of 2000. Now, the objection is in relation to the first statement, and I have the following points to make. My learned friend says there's no additional-- it doesn't really add anything. In fact, it's -- the first statement is the most detailed statement about what the witness saw and experienced in the municipality. Much of what's in the statement is actually a direct recounting of what happened in meetings that he personally participated in. The witness is able to come here and affirm the contents of his statement, and of course he's open to cross-examination. Further, it has been the practice of this Chamber to allow such AID statements to be admitted, and then obviously allow counsel to cross-examine on what they might think is speculation or otherwise. And finally, in relation to 92 bis, the AID statement does not mention Mr. Krajisnik, and therefore does not -- would not breach even by analogy any interpretation of the Rule 92 bis, and nor would it breach 89(F). Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you said that the Bosnian statement had all the hallmarks of 92 bis. You hear that Ms. Karagiannakis says that it fits well in the limits put by 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point I was making there, of course, is that there are -- there are -- there are certain aspects that must be covered to make a statement admissible under 92 bis, the certifying officer and what have you, and the various matters that are contained within the rule, and that those are the matters that I'm referring to. As to the other points that are made by Ms. Karagiannakis, I think that the point of substance that I wish to make is there is a world of difference between, as Your Honours will note from your experience of these statements, a world of difference between the manner in which a statement a taken by the offices of the International Criminal Tribunal and the statements taken by AID. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, if the Prosecution wishes to proceed under 89(F), I would submit that the evidence should be listed in the usual viva voce form as opposed to attempting to rely on the shortened 89(F) procedure by tendering both the ICTY and the AID statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask you then the following: 92 bis is not limited to ICTY statements, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, it isn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. And the second question I would have is that the whole specific procedure for 92 bis in respect of presiding officers, et cetera, of course, if the witness appears and will give his testimony mainly viva voce, although elements under 89(F) are confirmed by the witness, then, of course, I would say there's a whole Bench who could put the same questions to the witness as usually are put to the witness by a 92 bis presiding officer because that officer, of course, plays a very important role if the witness does not appear, nor for examination-in-chief nor for cross-examination. So would we miss anything if we would put the same questions to the witness if he appears here as a viva voce witness, compared to what a presiding officer confronts the witness with?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course in essence, I suppose that was the view of the majority in the case in question. But I think that the points made by Judge Hunt in his dissenting opinion in relation to the nature of evidence in chief are worth noting. And particularly, the point he makes about the fact that there's often a world of difference between what appears in black and white on a piece and what actually the witness attests to once they get into a witness box, and the subject to a proper evidence, nonleading evidence in chief. And it's on that basis, on the basis of substance, Your Honour, that I maintain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand since you rely not only on the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond decision but also on the observations made in the dissenting opinion of Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having read both statements and the -- being informed about the additional information sheet, the Chamber considers that we could proceed with this witness also under 89(F). But as far as the summary is concerned, I haven't seen it, would there be any agreement between the parties on what the summary -- which, of course, is again not a summary which is mainly for evidentiary purposes but to inform the public -- can we expect that the parties can agree on how to inform the public on what's in the 89(F) summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've discussed the summary and my learned friend had an objection. I've excised that part that was objected to, and I think we can proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I'm happy to proceed on that basis as Ms. Karagiannakis indicates and I foreshadowed earlier, we have had this discussion about the summary. I have indicated that there is a particular phrase I want to excise. Ms. Karagiannakis has agreed to that in view of the fact that the summary is for the information of the public and is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then, we'll proceed. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I'll call you Witness 48 since the protective measures granted in respect of you in another case continue to have their effect in this case. That means that we'll use a pseudonym, 48, Witness 48, and that facial distortion is effective. That means that no one sees your face in the outside world. Before giving evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Let me just check whether the facial distortion is effective. It is effective. Ms. Karagiannakis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the statements of 31 March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, would the pseudonym sheet not be the logical first one to be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just -- without saying anything else, could you just confirm that the details contained there are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that pseudonym sheet would have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P302 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the information here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness please be shown the statements of 31 March, 26 and 3rd November -- 21 March 1998, 26 and 3rd November 1999, and the additional memorandum dated 26 June 2000 in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, you said the 26th of June. I have a different date on my...

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could those statements please be given numbers. And I should foreshadow with the Court that they would be, if admitted, exhibits under seal as they identify the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, to the extent necessary. Would you please review them and see whether in all respects.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: We can undertake, Your Honour, to -- I can undertake to do the necessary redactions so there is a public version available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be preferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Witness do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be -- well, perhaps we go in chronological order. The first one is the 31st of March 1998. That would be...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P303.A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next one would be the 2000, the memorandum of conversation, 29th of June 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the next one is the 1999 ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, your idea of chronology is better than mine, Ms. Karagiannakis. The next one would then be the 26th of August and 3rd of November 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P303.B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one would then be the 29th of June 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the additional information sheet, I take it, Ms. Karagiannakis, would be dealt with in viva voce testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look at the statements in front of you. Do you recognise these statements as statements that you have given to Bosnian authorities and representatives of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify these statements as statements that I did give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review these statements prior to today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity of reviewing them before testifying today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that these statements are a correct and accurate -- are correct and accurate and that you are willing to confirm that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes. They are a correct reflection of what I want to confirm today before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I now propose to read out a summary in open session of this -- of the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The witness states that the president of the SDS in Bosanska Krupa was Miroslav Vjestica. He was also a representative of the party at the republican level. Another member of the SDS who held a high position was Gojko Klickovic. The witness states that Gojko Klickovic appeared to be in the coordinator for SDS activities in the area of Bosanska Krupa and that he seemed to be the most important person in the SDS in the operational sense. A crisis staff was formed by the SDS in Bosanska Krupa before the start of the war. In September 1991, Milan Martic was arrested and taken to the police station at Bosanska Otoka. This caused commotion and civil unrest amongst the Bosniak population. The Serbs had organised a paramilitary group in the hills and had threatened to attack Bosanska Krupa if Martic was not released. Martic was subsequently released. After the release of Martic, Gojko Klickovic went to the field to tell Serb paramilitaries in the surrounding area that Martic had been released, and therefore they no longer had to threaten Bosanska Krupa. Klickovic stated that the local SDS had 5.000 armed men under its control. During 1991, Biljana Plavsic came to Bosanska Krupa. During this visit, she met with the local SDS. In 1992, a proposal was put forward by the SDS about the division of the municipality. They asked for a separate Serbian Bosanska Krupa to be established. The SDS produced a document in the form of a programme asking the -- asking for the division of the territory into Serb and non-Serb areas. On 20 April 1992, paramilitaries surrounded the Bosniak village of Arapusa. Klickovic was asked to explain to the forces that the state was functioning and that the law would take its proper role but he did not do so. He told the commander of the paramilitary forces to remain at their positions. On 20 April 1992 a meeting was held in the municipal building. The people present included Fikret Abdic, a member of the Bosnian-Hercegovina Presidency; Klickovic, Vjestica, the president and vice-president of the SDA. Klickovic and Vjestica once again requested a division. They said that running the municipality in tandem, living together, was out of the question. They wanted to have Serb territory, and the Serbian people had voted for them to work towards that aim. Serbian children should learn Serbian history, Serbian books, et cetera. It was agreed that there would be another meeting that evening at Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond 9.30 p.m. However, the SDS members did not show up for that meeting. That night, the Serbs were particularly active in evacuating the town. On 21 April 1992, none of the senior officials of Serb ethnicity showed up for work at the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, I notice that the -- at least the French translation which I can follow is already a few lines behind, and that's -- they are not to be blamed for that. So could you please adapt your speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The witness was told by citizens and observers that paramilitary units had started assembling on the hills around the town. Serb citizens were leaving the town in droves. Immediately after the JNA commander, General Ninkovic, left the municipality building on that day, the Serbs started shelling the town with mortars from all directions. Once the shelling started, people in the town started to flee towards Cazin and Bihac. After the attack started, spontaneous resistance was put up by local people with hunting weapons, and 70 police with about 200 reserve police. This lasted about four days and allowed 90 per cent of the population to flee from the town. The witness crossed over to the left bank of the Una River on 21 April 1992. He saw the town of Bosanska Krupa burning from the other side of the river. The Serbs kept the entire right bank of the River Una and expelled the non-Serb population from the town and villages on the right bank. The property of the Bosniaks in houses and flats on the right side of the river was looted. 12 civilians were killed in the first wave of the attack on the town. Many people were taken to Jasenica camp and later to the Petar Kocic primary school in Bosanska Krupa. On 23rd April 1992, there were renewed negotiations which took place in Bosanski Petrovac. Vjestica was the SDS representative from Bosanska Krupa. At the meeting, the participants discussed how to stop the conflict and make a buffer zone. The Serbs proposed that the border, that is, the line of separation, be the River Una, and that the buffer zone should be manned by JNA units or by Stojan Zupljanin's police force which would come from Banja Luka, and also the municipal police. Three or four meetings were held around that time, but nothing was resolved. The SDS was in a more favourable position than if the SDA had agreed to all of their demands, and it was clear that the SDS was not prepared to give back the area they had seized. In 1995, the Bosnian Army successfully retook the areas of Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovac, and Sanski Most. The witness returned and saw that the mosque and the 400-year-old Catholic church had been destroyed. The orthodox church showed bullet damage but was not destroyed and still remains in the town today. All of the Muslim villages and whole areas of Muslim housing in the town which were of no military significance were destroyed. That concludes the summary, Your Honour. If we could go into private session. And the basis for this, Your Honour, is I'm is going to be asking the witness to provide the bases upon which he says certain things in his statement, and this would possibly require him to recount meetings at which he was present with a limited amount of other people which, taken together, could identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would like to go into private session right away to start with. Then we'll first go into private session. 3 Witness 48, perhaps I explain to you a bit of the procedure. Ms. 4 Karagiannakis has just read out a summary of what is in your written 5 statements. That is to inform the public about those elements of the 6 evidence that are not repeated in this courtroom, but of course the 7 public should know what the evidence is about. We'll now turn into 8 private session because you'll be asked a few questions on meetings 9 and perhaps the answers to those questions might identify you as a 10 person. So therefore, we go now into private session. That means that the outside world doesn't hear what you will say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now move into open session. And I have to clarify that already on the basis of your request to move into private session that we moved into private session. But then, of course, in private session, the Chamber granted your request. And therefore, we remained in private session in order not to give any identifying element -- not to make any identifying element public during the testimony. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just confirm that -- confirm that that map shows the position and border of Bosanska Krupa before the war started.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, this map does show the position of the Municipality of Bosanska Krupa before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please now be shown map 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P305.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you take a pen and mark with the number 1 the location of Arapusa village, a blue pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that being shown -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. Is that being shown on the monitor, the map? Could you please indicate on the map to your left-hand side by marking it with the number 1 in blue pen the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, the question is whether we can use your computer programme and the ELMO at the same time, or whether that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, in these circumstances, we can simply use the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we use the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Court how far away Arapusa village was from Bosanska Krupa town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: If you're asking me, Arapusa is about 18 kilometres from the town of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: It's a village inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: The surrounding villages were Serbian ones. The population of those villages was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm going to now ask the witness a question about his role in relation to this village which could result in him being identified. So I ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Karagiannakis, I will grant your request, but not after having asked you another question about maps. It's not the first time that this happens. You provide us with one map without scale, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you provide us with another map with a scale on it. If you compare the contours of the large map of the Bosanska Krupa Municipality, if you compare that with the contours of the Bosanska Krupa Municipality on the map with the scale, you'll see that the second one is a projection. If you just look at Bosanska Krupa south to north on the small map, it is more kilometres or more distance than from east to west. However, on the other map, east to west is longer than south to north. That means that one of the two maps is not precise. And if that would be the map with the scale on it, then it's of no use to have a scale on it because it's a projected map. So therefore, it's not the first time. It happened in Sanski Most as well. So in order to get the right impression of distances, perhaps precise maps, not projected ones, would have to be preferred. This is just a general observation I made -- I make at this moment. It's not a reason to immediately change them all. But everyone should be aware that these maps are printed on a different basis. We'll now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to the topic of the attack on Bosanska Krupa town on the 21st of April and its after-effects. At paragraph 39 of your 1999 statement you state that citizens had told you that paramilitaries had surrounded the town on 21 April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: I apologise. What was the number of the paragraph in the statement from 1999?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1999, paragraph 39. And also, please, look at paragraph 2 of the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also now look at the paragraph 2 of the 2000 memorandum.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you provided some additional information about that point, and you say in that paragraph "I do not see the units for myself. I was in the municipality with observers, and they told us -- they told us and they said the soldiers did not have the dress code of ordinary soldiers." Now, could you please tell us who were the observers you were referring to in the 2000 statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: They were representatives of the United Nations, in fact. They were people in white clothes. They had previously come to the municipality. Their uniforms were completely white. And on the whole, they would discuss the situation in the field. These people came a little earlier on that day, and they were there from 10.00 in the morning -- they were in my office from 10.00 in the morning. But at the time of the attack, they took out protective equipment from their bags. I don't know whether they were expecting something or whether this was their usual equipment that they had. But I know that they put on flak jackets and other items that served to protect people in such situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you just said that they were representatives of the United Nations. And in paragraph 39 that's in front of you, you refer to ECMM monitors. Were both of those groups there, or would you like to clarify that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Well, look, all the people who came from the outside, all the foreigners, we frequently mixed up these terms. We frequently mixed up the United Nations and the European Community. For us, they were observers on the whole, and we didn't make any significant distinction between UN representatives and representatives of the EC. Perhaps they were from the EC, but this wasn't of any particular importance for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: I'd like to add that they were not armed. They weren't representatives of the military. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you to paragraph 17 of your 1998 statement. And there you describe the shelling of the town. You've also described it at paragraph 43 of your 1999 statement. Now, in this paragraph, the first line, it states "the first shell was fired on the town from Serbian positions" -- sorry, "the first shell was fired on the town from Serbian positions fell shortly after General Ninkovic left towards Jasenica." Now, did you personally witness the shelling of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I was an eyewitness of the shelling of the town. My official car which was an Audi 100, it was white and parked in front of the municipal building, this car was the first thing to be hit. The bonnet was hit, and it was no longer possible to use it. So I crossed over to the other bank on foot. I've just remembered another detail I would like to mention. I found a piece of shrapnel which ended up at my feet. When I lifted it up, it was still hot. So this was material proof that it wasn't a dream. It was reality, and a very terrible reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 17, it states that the first shell was fired from Serbian positions. What's the basis for your knowledge of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: When you said from Serbian positions, I have to explain the location of Bosanska Krupa. Bosanska Krupa is in a valley. And the surrounding hills are inhabited by Serbs, especially the part in the direction of Grmec. So we could call them positions or something else, but that is where they were physically present. They lived in those areas. On the other hand, it wasn't possible for an attack to be launched from the other side because no one else had such weapons. So I couldn't go to check whether those positions were there, but I'm sure that they were there and had such weapons because only they had such weapons at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please look at paragraph 45 of your 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It states that once the shelling started, people in the town started to flee towards Cazin and Bihac. Now, as far as you knew the people that were fleeing, can you tell us what ethnicity they were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Citizens of Bosniak nationality were fleeing, although not everyone fled in that direction. There were some people who didn't have a sense of direction. There were people who were in a state of shock. And there were others who didn't flee at all; they didn't want to go anywhere. But most of the people who fled were people of Bosniak nationality, and they fled in this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned other people who didn't flee at all. Did you subsequently learn what happened to those other people that didn't flee at all? And if you did learn, can you tell us how you know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: The people who didn't flee anywhere, the people who remained in the houses were taken away to camps later on. And exchanges were arranged for certain people. I know about this because my mother was one of those people. My aunt, my uncle as well. Many of my relatives didn't want to flee, and they were, in fact, expelled. They had to leave their homes, and they were taken to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Just one last question before the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned here a number of your relatives. Without mentioning any of their names, please, can you tell me whether to your knowledge any of these people were involved in any military activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: No, none of them were. On the whole, these were people who weren't fit for military service, and they did not take part in military activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That might be a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Ms. Karagiannakis. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, witness, you mentioned that your relatives had told you about what had happened at the municipality after the takeover. Could you tell -- please tell me what the ethnicity of your relatives who told you was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: All my relatives who remained in Bosanska Krupa and who were later expelled were Muslims, Bosniaks by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 22 of your 1998 statement and paragraph 54 of your 1999 statement, you say that 12 civilians were killed during the attack, initial attack on Bosanska Krupa. How did you come to know about these 12 civilians that were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: On the basis of information brought in by the civilians who had been expelled and also the representatives -- well, I'm going to refer to them as representatives of the international community, whether they were European officers or whoever, but anyway, representatives of the international community who had an insight into the situation, on the basis of what they told us, I came to learn that there were dead people out in the streets. And we decided that on the 6th of May, two completely identical groups on both sides, that is to say, representatives of the international community and representatives of the civilian powers and authorities, the Red Cross, and the medical corps, that we would meet in front of the department store and take the necessary equipment to collect up the bodies of the people lying around Bosanska Krupa. So this meeting was supposed to take place on the 6th of May, and we set out in the number provided for and with all the members present and ready. However, when we arrived at the tunnel, the railway tunnel just before the bridge, the shelling and shooting started. And we were stopped in our intentions of proceeding further. And the vehicle was hit, a vehicle belonging to the international community that was transporting us. And we took refuge in the tunnel. We sheltered in the tunnel. And then the officer who was the representative of the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond international community contacted the other side where there was also his counterpart, another officer of the international community. The code name was Echo Charlie. I remember that. And Gojko Klickovic at the time gave orders, or rather said there were no operations underway and no drive to collect up dead bodies could go ahead. So he didn't allow us to get to the meeting point and put our plans into practice to collect up the bodies. The civilians who had been killed were later on -- their bodies were brought in to the Cazin Municipality where they were buried. And I attended the funeral. There were 12 bodies. 12 people were buried on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go into private session now, Your Honour. I would like to ask the witness about a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps before doing so, is it the position of the Prosecution that these are -- because we haven't heard any further details about people that were killed. It could be all kind of circumstances under which they were killed. Is that -- is it the position of the Prosecution that it's intentional killing of civilians, or is it -- it could be collateral damage of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The information the Prosecution has -- is provided by the Prosecution, which is in paragraph 22 of the 1998 statement and 54 of the 1999 statement which is -- which the witness has recounted now. Those are the only details we intend to lead about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: From this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From this witness. I do understand. Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's confirmed on my screen that we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to a different topic, which is intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before testifying here today, did you have an opportunity to listen to intercepted communications, and did you identify the voices of the participants as being Miroslav Vjestica and Radovan Karadzic in one conversation, and Miroslav Vjestica and Momcilo Krajisnik in the second conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes. I did identify the people you mentioned yesterday when I listened to the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next exhibit, which is a declaration. It contains the witness's name, so it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P306 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I should explain for the benefit of the Court that the witness should be shown the declaration, but the declaration is the first in a package which contains the intercepted communications in both languages, and an audio CD of those communications. But I don't propose to ask him about the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's just -- it's the first in a package. You mean that other intercepts will follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No, these are the only two intercepts. It's just -- it's his declaration about the voice recognition, and then followed by what he has recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to this, Your Honour, I understand that this exhibit is purely for the purposes of voice identification. I would make one point at this juncture, Your Honour, and that is that, of course, we've heard evidence from the witness in relation to his contacts with the person, Mr. Vjestica. But Your Honour, I don't think that in the circumstances the witness is in a position based on personal knowledge to identify the voices of either Mr. Radovan Karadzic or Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, whether or not you can cross-examine the witness on that, I can tell you, Ms. Loukas, that even although I never met Pavarotti I certainly would recognise his voice for other reasons. So it's not as such because he never met someone --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, Your Honour. But nevertheless I think we must always apply the best-evidence rule, and the best evidence in relation to questions of voice is from somebody who is actually had considerably more personal knowledge of the person than the witness has had. I just put that marker down so Your Honour is aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that might require under circumstances that you'd need two witnesses to identify voices. But for the time being -- the best-evidence rule, of course, which is well known in the common-law tradition does not in exactly the same way operate in this Tribunal. But it certainly -- it's something to be aimed at to try to find the best evidence for whatever you want to establish.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, indeed, Your Honour. I mean, The situation is, of course, when we're dealing with this sort of -- the hybrid nature of the Tribunal and the combination of common-law principles and civil-law principles, nevertheless whilst the Tribunal can inform itself in any way it sees fit, nevertheless they are matters that go very importantly to the probative nature of the evidence in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly may has some effect on the probative value and weighing the evidence. One second, please. Yes, I just reread your objection. You may proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the declaration that -- the declaration in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this declaration bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes. My signature is on the declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it attest as to the -- your voice identification on these two intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, it does attest to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I've concluded with that exhibit, Your Honour. If the witness could be shown the next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These exhibits are to be returned to -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, as far as the numbers are concerned, could you please assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript of the intercept dated 24/06/1991 will be P306.A. And the transcript of the intercept conversation of 05/06/1991 will be P306.B. And the CD of the intercepts, P306.C. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And this exhibit, P307.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that CD, I'm just wondering if the Prosecution might have a spare copy of that particular CD for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, that an audio was sent to the Defence. However, we will endeavour to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I first ask you, Ms. Loukas, the transfer of the CD to the Detention Unit yesterday, finally was it successful, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It was successful, Your Honour, unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it in relation to this that you would like to have a spare copy, or is it -- has it -- is it totally unrelated?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Your Honour, the -- Ms. Cmeric tells me that we don't have a CD, a separate CD of the nature that was just tendered to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: We'll endeavour to assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find a practical solution for that. Thank you for your cooperation. Then Madam Registrar, the next exhibit, P307, is that a report on the work of the Municipal Assembly and War Presidency from the 1st of January 1992 to the 20th of April 1993 in a draft version?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have a chance to review this document prior to your testimony in the Brdjanin case and also prior to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a chance to review this document prior to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: The author of this document is Gojko Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: We already discussed the document that the SDS officially sent to the Municipality of Bosanska Krupa as a plan for the municipality's division. I had insight into that document. And many of the elements contained in that document is contained in this report. In fact, I recognise the rhetorics of Gojko Klickovic, the way he speaks, because he worked with me, and we cooperated frequently, sat together, discussed matters, that kind of thing, so that judging by the expressions used in this report I recognise his style and the way he spoke, his words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer that many elements contained in the proposal for the separation of the municipality that was presented to you prior to the conflict are similar to those in this document. Could you take the Court to the parts that are similar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Mention is made here of the economic reasons, the economic reasons are stated for the separation of the municipality and the political work needed. And then the reasons are enumerated, set out. Now, having known about these events and the contents of this, the only man who could know about all that was Gojko Klickovic. No other person in the SDS was in a position to know things of this kind. So in my opinion, he was the only person who could have compiled a document of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned the economic reasons and the political reasons, are you referring to page -- the headings on page 2 of the B/C/S version and page 3 of the English version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it. On page 2, you have the basic reasons set out for compiling the project on the municipality's partitioning, so that's the element dating to before the war. And now, this is just slightly rearranged, but basically it's identical. The report is identical to, or rather it confirms the justification for the municipality's partitioning or separation. In fact, we are dealing here with 1993 and the prospects, or rather Gojko Klickovic's visions are quite different here because in 1993, he was the victor, so the prospects and his visions were well known if the situation remained the same as it was in 1993. So he had every reason to write a report of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could I just take you to the third reason under the political reasons that's stated there, and it says "the case involving the Branko Copic monument, which goes beyond mere opposition to the erection of the monument." Can you tell us what happened in relation to the Branko Copic monument? You'll find that point 3, B/C/S version, page 2, under the second underlined heading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that portion. The case involving Branko Copic took on rather broad dimensions, and for me, it was a very difficult case because I was under pressure from the public. In fact, I was facing a dilemma myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just stop you there. Can you please tell us who Branko Copic was and what the proposal was in relation to the monument.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Branko Copic was a poet. He had sympathisers throughout Yugoslavia. He was a partisan poet. And he had a broad following amongst all the nations and nationalities or ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As he was born in Bosanska Krupa, he was particularly celebrated and respected in Bosanska Krupa. So the opposition to erecting a monument of that kind, regardless of the fact that it might not have been -- that it might have been illegal in terms of procedure to put the monument up, was very risky business. The SDS wanted to erect such a monument on the basis of some illegal paperwork compiled by Mr. Miroslav Vjestica who was the head of the town planning department previously, and therefore had the possibility of implementing a project of that kind. So I had the dilemma of whether I should forget the fact that the process might not be legitimate and to accept it, or to oppose it. I decided to oppose it because if the monument had been erected, there would have been scope for further acts of that kind in the municipality which would lead to unforeseen consequences. So I was conscious of the risk because not many people would have noted opposition to the legality or not. And there were strong attacks and criticisms from journalists in Belgrade. They tried to depict me as somebody who was against Branko Copic, and by the same token against the Serbian people and so on and so forth. In order to overcome this impasse or the situation, we sought a solution in Sarajevo, and this time, once again, we went to Sarajevo to find that solution. We went to see Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik at the time who was the president of the assembly. And I think that Radovan Karadzic was involved in the case as well. However, I didn't meet him in Sarajevo at the time. We only talked to the president of the assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik. But we weren't able to solve the issue on that occasion, and it is my feeling that they understood what it was all about. And so the case died a natural death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Copic monument actually erected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: The monument was illegally erected, but the municipal organs ordered the public utilities company from Bosanska Krupa to remove the monument and place it in a warehouse. So the monument was removed from that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the first point under number 2, political reasons, it mentions the SDA's policy. As a member of the SDA, can you tell us what -- can you comment on that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for the remainder of this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 55 of your 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: I've found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There you refer to RS currency as an example of your statement the process of taking over areas and making them part of the RS seemed to be well coordinated. Witness, could you look at the last exhibit and just confirm that that's the currency that you refer to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P308.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is an example of the currency in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court why you say that supports your statement that this showed taking over areas and making them part of the RS seemed to be well coordinated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 48
utterances.text: Well, look, in 1992 I didn't have the possibility of ordering certain events chronologically, but I was in a position to do so in 1995. So this is a comment I made by chance. I came by these bills. By following the events from 1992 to 1995, I put the events in order, and I came to the conclusion that there was a way in which the Serbs coordinated their efforts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in 1992, a bill was issued, and it contained the words "the National Bank of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina." In 1995, the military situation was completely different. And in political terms, Bosnia and Herzegovina could no longer be contained as part of the name of the bank issuing the hundred thousand dinar bill. So this was a stage. And it is on this basis that I came to the conclusion that there had been coordination and that there had been a plan to do things in the way that they were actually done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I should just indicate, I'm just marking this at this point, that I do, in fact, object to that first sentence of paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And reasons for your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I take it as is usually the case, we argue these objections in full at the end of the witness's evidence. It's perhaps not appropriate that I give the objection in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can do it now, but not in front of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I wasn't aware of the nature of your objection. Perhaps we could do it at the end of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That's the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the end --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: This is the end of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I add something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's something you think to be of importance which you would like to tell us, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, when we follow the events that unfolded, when I claim that there was coordination, this can be supported by what happened in Slavonski Brod, in Dubica, in Prijedor. Territory was conquered in a controlled manner, the territory that was given the name "Republika Srpska." And this all culminated in Prijedor. Things came to a head in Prijedor when they organised the assemblies of the two republics of Serbia from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they supported the unification of the western Serbian lands. I had the opportunity of following that assembly in the territory of the so-called Bihac pocket. And at the time, I, in fact, understood what the Serbs' plan in that area was because Martic also attended the assembly that was held in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what you wanted to add. Ms. Karagiannakis, before we proceed, I'm just trying to fully understand the evidence given in relation to the bank notes. The witness testified about bank notes of 1992, and I see that one of the bank notes, the 5.000 dinar, is of 1992. The other one, the 100.000 bank note seems to be from 1993. The witness testified about -- well, the issuing authority, and I wonder whether in the 5.000 dinar bank note that we would find that just on the other side of the bank note rather than on this one. But I'm not quite sure. I'm trying to decipher, the 100.000 on top, at least I see there's something like "Republika Srpska." That's 1993. But on the other, I have some difficulties to identify anything else than the 5.000 dinars which seems to be at the bottom, dark line. I also see that it's issued in Banja Luka and under whose authority. But I cannot find, as a matter of fact, the name of the bank issuing this money, and that should be the National Bank of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So would that be on the other side of the 5.000 dinar bank note?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the photocopy I have in front of me, and if we look at Banja Luka, the 5.000 dinar note is at the top. And at the bottom it says Banja Luka 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: In the top right-hand corner of my copy, I can make out "Narodna Banka Srpske Republike Bosne i Hercegovine". So it looks like on the copy that I have, above the shield, it identifies the issuing authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just have a look at your copy to see whether it's the same as the copy we have. Couldn't it be nice to provide the Chamber with the same sides of the bank notes that you are holding in your hands because you are -- exactly what I expected. You are looking at the back side of the copy that we have. It would really be of assistance to look at the same pictures as you seem to because -- is this the one you wanted to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't. Could I just have -- could it be returned to Ms. Karagiannakis, and could we perhaps after the break seek verification with the witness whether this is the back side. But -- or Madam Registrar, could I please inspect everything in relation to the bank notes that has been given to the... I have to apologise, Ms. Karagiannakis, because it seems that we -- that the back side of the bank notes were not distributed to the Chamber. So we saw only one side of the bank notes, and that's exactly the side on which I had difficulties to find confirmation of what the witness testified. You will agree with me that the exception confirms the rule that our registrar is the most precise one in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's now perfectly clear to me. It was not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps before the Chamber gives an opportunity to Ms. Loukas to start cross-examination, perhaps we could have an early break today and ask the witness to leave the courtroom so that Ms. Loukas is in a position to make further submissions in relation to the objection you made.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's just one further matter, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be dealt with in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, probably shouldn't be, Your Honour. The witness can either leave or remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if we would have a break anyhow, do we need the witness if you address the matter you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a matter I wish to address now in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But should the witness remain standby, or can we, if we have an early break, could we continue after the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond break so that the witness is now excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's the point I want to deal with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes it's -- may I first ask you, do you understand any English or do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't speak English. And I understand very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I nevertheless have to ask you just to leave the courtroom for a second because sometimes issues have to be dealt with in the absence of the witness. So may I ask you to follow the usher for this moment. But to remain standby. We, of course, first have to pull the curtains down. Ms. Loukas, the audio is open. Should we pull the curtains again, and then pull them down again, or is it something that we could deal with even if no one sees us?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I often get the feeling that in view of the absence of the public in the public gallery, that it's not going to make a great deal of difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be practical for one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, just to indicate in relation to this particular witness and the question of the cross-examination, as Your Honour is aware, the Defence up until yesterday was dealing with Mr. Kljuic, and we, of course, haven't had an opportunity to speak with Mr. Krajisnik in relation to this particular witness. And more specifically, we only received yesterday afternoon when we got out of Court the supplemental information sheet which specifically mentions Mr. Krajisnik. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, I would want to have the opportunity to have a conference with my client prior to commencing the cross-examination. So therefore, we would need a longer than the usual 15- or 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that can be arranged, this meeting, during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I should think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: At this point it's a little bit difficult to determine. The alternative, because we are ahead of schedule at the moment of course, is we could always start the cross-examination tomorrow. We could finish early today, I could go and see Mr. Krajisnik at the UNDU this afternoon, and we could begin and finish the cross-examination tomorrow. Or I can take a longer than usual break now, have a conference with Mr. Krajisnik, and then commence the cross-examination this afternoon. I'm in Your Honours' hands. Because at this stage, we are of course ahead of schedule in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be the best solution at this moment to finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if that would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That would be suitable. That would allow me the opportunity to have a conference with Mr. Krajisnik at the United Nations Detention Unit this afternoon, and there's of course no way I would need the entire day tomorrow in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could then also raise the issue of next Tuesday's witness where you said something about --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just having received the material this morning, Your Honour, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then first of all, I'd like to explain this to the witness. But just for the time being. There was another issue you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. There was the question of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we do the following: We first, since the curtains are down, we invite the witness to come back and explain to him that we will continue tomorrow morning. And then we'll pull the curtains up again, and then you make your objection in relation to the-- or should it be done in private session, or any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't propose to in any way refer to the witness in a way that might identify him for the purposes of the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then do it very practically. Madam Usher, could you then please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the parties will agree that I explain to the witness without pulling the curtains high and then pulling them down again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- no, it's not -- let's keep them down. Witness, in your absence, the Defence has requested to have a break now and to start your cross-examination tomorrow. The Chamber has listened to the reasons and the practicalities. Since we would not finish your cross-examination anyhow today and since there's no risk, I would say, that we would not finish by tomorrow, the Chamber has decided that you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence starting tomorrow morning, 9.00, but in Courtroom III, I think, Madam Registrar -- no, that's for next Monday. Same courtroom, yes. So you're excused for the remaining part of the day. I want to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give. And we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was a bit late with my instructions to -- well, perhaps, we could have all parties assist in having the curtains up again. Ms. Loukas, sometimes unexpected things do happen. Ms. Loukas, you would like to raise an objection in relation to a certain paragraph of the written statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. Just in relation to, as I foreshadowed, that first sentence of paragraph 55. Your Honour, the witness has given his evidence in chief that might go towards supporting that particular proposition, and I would submit, Your Honour, that that sort of evidence is of negligible probative value, that sort of sweeping generalisations of that nature are not helpful in terms of the fact-finding exercise that the Trial Chamber must determine and should, in fact, be avoided as part of the evidence taking into account the balancing act that Your Honours must perform under Rule 89 of the Rules of the Tribunal. And in those circumstances, having heard the evidence in chief of the witness that goes towards supporting or otherwise that particular statement, I would submit that a statement of that nature has next-to-no probative value in the circumstances and should be excised from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection, as I understand it, goes to the weight and not the actual admissibility of the evidence. The second thing I would like to note is that the witness has indeed given evidence and he has described the basis for that conclusion so that that conclusion must be seen in light of the witness's evidence. And Your Honours are able to judge that and give it the appropriate weight. So it's not really an issue of admissibility, but weight, and therefore that should not be struck from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're just relating -- you're just talking about the first line of 55 where the witness, I think, added a few elements for this conclusion which, of course, then in the oral testimony, the conclusion, if it is given additional support, is in evidence anyhow. So I'm just wondering at the practical level if we take it out of the 89(F) statement, then it would be in the oral testimony anyhow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. But I think perhaps it's -- perhaps it might be appropriate for the Trial Chamber to give an indication as to what sort of weight the Trial Chamber would give a statement of that nature in view of the sweeping generalised nature of the statement, in view of the nature of the witness's evidence. It's my submission, Your Honour, that evidence of this nature is not the sort of evidence that the Trial Chamber would use as a basis for forming the requisite fact-finding exercise the Trial Chamber must determine. And in those circumstances, perhaps an indication could be given by the Trial Chamber which would be, I think, helpful to both the Prosecution and Defence as to the approach to be adopted by the Trial Chamber in relation to sweeping generalisations and almost baseless generalisations of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I look at the first line which is a sweeping statement to the extent that it covers the process of taking over areas and making them part of Republika Srpska and then qualifies it as coordinated it, whereas the support only deals with a specific element of coordination, in the additional testimony by the witness, he added some other elements, I think the statement as such, the first line, of course, will be interpreted by the Chamber on the basis of the support given. I mean, if there would have been no mentioning of bank notes or what happened elsewhere or nothing at all, then of course the statement as such would not really be of great assistance to establish what happened. What we see is that there's a link between the first line because limits of the sweeping statement are found in the support given to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber will certainly keep that in mind that on the basis of bank notes, you could not establish coordinated -- coordinated taking over of areas and making them part of. I mean, this is a small element, so certainly in order to come to the kind of conclusions the witness comes, one would need far more and a lot of other information as well, and not just the bank notes. So to that extent, the weight of this evidence, also of the first line, will be directly linked to the factual support given to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then still then insist on taking out the first line?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's adequate for my purposes at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the explanation is you don't insist on --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Clearly the important aspect is the reliance on the actual evidence given by the witness as opposed to sweeping opinions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other procedural issue to be discussed at this moment? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just thinking that we probably will be done before the full component of the time tomorrow, and I didn't know if the Court wanted to have us prepare to deal with any housekeeping matters, or since Monday is going to be a housekeeping day any way, if we'll finish early tomorrow and just finish then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if we finish early tomorrow, would you prefer to deal with all the housekeeping matters or to think them over over the weekend and then to deal with them on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I must say I think Monday is probably a better idea, Your Honour, because I think we have a whole series of matters that have been left outstanding that we probably, I think the Prosecution and I in conjunction with the updated exhibit list with the Registrar, I think we need to go over in some detail to ensure that this particular housekeeping day, as it were, is most effective. So we cover those loose ends rather than sort of deal with them in a halfhearted sort of way on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will very much appreciate if you could give a list of housekeeping matters to deal with on Monday, and of course if you provided them we could compare it with our list of housekeeping matters to be dealt with. Then we adjourn for the day until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of October, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.09 p.m.,
